title: Mystery: a Secret Now Revealed
lead: The Greek mysterion in the Bible is not a puzzle but a secret of God that was hidden and has now been made known. Daniel uses it of Nebuchadnezzar's dream; Paul uses it of God's plan in Christ, above all that Gentiles are fellow heirs with Israel (Ephesians 3:3-6). The Latin Bible translated it sacramentum, which is how marriage came to be called a sacrament.

sections.b: In the Greek of Daniel, mysterion translates the Aramaic raz, a hidden thing that God reveals through a dream and its interpretation (Daniel 2:18-19, 27-30, 47). The Dead Sea Scrolls use raz for secrets of God's plan that the Teacher of Righteousness was given to read in the prophets (1QpHab 7:1-5). Paul takes up this setting: the mystery is hidden in the ages, made known by revelation, and has to do with the end of the age (Romans 16:25-26; 1 Corinthians 2:7; 1 Corinthians 15:51; Ephesians 3:3-9; Colossians 1:26-27).
sections.refs: Daniel 2:18-19; Daniel 2:47; Romans 11:25; Romans 16:25-26; 1 Corinthians 2:7; 1 Corinthians 15:51; Ephesians 1:9; Ephesians 3:3-9; Ephesians 5:32; Colossians 1:26-27

sections.b: The Latin translators rendered mysterion as sacramentum in Ephesians 5:32 and elsewhere, and from that word the church's "sacraments" took part of their name. The Eastern churches still speak of the "mysteries" for what the West calls sacraments. The mystery religions of Greece (such as Eleusis) kept secret rites, but the New Testament mystery is the opposite: a secret that is announced to everyone.
